title: The role of Artificial Intelligence in Transforming Higher Education
extended_summary:
This thesis examines how artificial intelligence is transforming higher education, with particular attention to pedagogical practice, student equity, and academic integrity. It asks how AI is changing teaching and learning, and what the implications are for fairness and institutional governance across diverse learning environments. The motivation is the rapid spread of generative AI, learning analytics, intelligent tutoring systems, and other AI tools, alongside concerns about bias, privacy, overreliance, and unequal access.

The study uses a case study of a single university, supported by a literature review, stakeholder surveys, qualitative interviews, document analysis, and analysis of academic performance and administrative efficiency metrics before and after AI integration. The context is higher education rather than school settings: participants include students, faculty, and administrators, with attention to disciplinary differences and digital inequality. The thesis also draws on frameworks such as responsible AI principles, the AI Literacy Heptagon, and the AI Assessment Scale to interpret adoption and governance.

The findings suggest that AI-based tutoring systems, early alert tools, learning analytics, and AI-assisted assessment can improve personalization, efficiency, and some outcomes such as dropout rates and response times. However, adoption varies by discipline and demographic group, and concerns remain about algorithmic bias, academic integrity, and uneven access to infrastructure and digital literacy. The thesis concludes that AI can improve learning and operational workflows when implemented with inclusive policy, ethical oversight, infrastructure support, and training, but that benefits must be balanced against equity risks.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods case study thesis with surveys, interviews, document analysis, and system logs, so it provides qualitative and correlational evidence rather than a controlled experiment. The design is informative but does not meet strong causal credibility criteria for blue or green tiers.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports broadly positive institutional and workflow effects, but the evidence is largely descriptive and no effect sizes are provided. The practical impact appears plausible yet modest and unclear in magnitude at the population level.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI chatbots and course assistants used by students for explanations, feedback, idea generation, writing support, and exam preparation in higher education settings.
AI-based learning analytics and early alert tools used to monitor student activity, predict performance, and reduce dropout risk through intervention signals.
Adaptive tutoring systems used for personalized learning support, student modeling, and step-by-step instructional guidance within university courses.
AI-supported formative assessment and feedback workflows that provide automated or semi-automated feedback on student work and learning progress.

finding.finding_summary: The thesis reports that AI integration improved institutional workflows, with reduced response times and improved administrative efficiency after AI adoption. It also suggests AI enhanced personalization and supported policy development, though outcomes varied by discipline and demographic group.
finding.measure: Administrative efficiency metrics, response times, dropout rates, stakeholder perceptions

finding.finding_summary: AI-based tutoring systems and early alert tools were associated with faster processing and more efficient academic support workflows. The paper specifically states that response times fell and that AI reduced administrative burden in the case university, but no numerical effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Response times, system usage logs, administrative processing time

finding.finding_summary: Student users reported favorable experiences with generative AI for explanations, feedback, and idea generation, suggesting improved engagement and perceived usefulness. However, the paper notes concerns about overreliance, academic integrity, and unequal access, so the overall pattern is positive but uneven.
finding.measure: Survey responses on adoption and perceived usefulness; interviews on student experiences

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can support critical thinking through scaffolding, but also warns that overreliance may undermine critical thinking and higher-order reasoning. This outcome is discussed conceptually and qualitatively rather than with a quantified test measure.
finding.measure: Interview themes and literature synthesis on critical thinking and agency
